title: Static Typing
body:
Every expression has a type that is known **before the program runs**, and a program whose
types do not fit does not compile. The contrast is dynamic typing, where values carry types and
the mismatch is discovered when execution reaches it, if it ever does.

```haskell
length "hello" + True     -- rejected at compile time: Int and Bool do not add
```

```javascript
"5" - 2        // 3          JavaScript coerces
"5" + 2        // "52"       and coerces differently for +
```

The [[JavaScript]] line is the standard argument for the other side of the table: nothing is
wrong until it is, and then the wrongness is a plausible-looking value rather than an error.

## The three axes people confuse

"Static" is one of three independent questions, and the vault's languages sit differently on
each:

| | When are types checked | How hard are they to subvert | Must you write them |
|---|---|---|---|
| [[C]] | compile time | **weakly**: [[Type casting\|cast]] around any of it | always |
| [[Java]] | compile time | strongly, with an escape hatch | always |
| [[JavaScript]] | run time | not applicable, coercion everywhere | never |
| [[Haskell]] | compile time | strongly, no cast exists | rarely ([[Type Inference]]) |

[[C]] is the row that makes the point. It is statically typed, and
`*(double *)&someInt` will happily reinterpret the bits, so its check is advisory. That is why
"static" on its own is a weak claim: what [[Haskell]] adds is that **there is no cast**, so a
value of type `Int` is an `Int` for the whole program and the compiler's conclusions cannot be
falsified later. See [[Atomic type]] and [[Variable]] for how the C side is written up.

## What it catches and what it costs

Caught before the program runs: argument order and arity mistakes, a `null`/`Nothing` you
forgot to handle (because [[Algebraic Data Type|`Maybe`]] forces the case split), an unhandled
constructor after you add one, and every use site of a function whose signature you just
changed. That last one is the underrated benefit: change a type and the compiler hands you the
complete list of places that now need attention, which no [[Unit testing|test suite]] can
promise.

The cost is honest and is the standard objection: **a type system rejects programs that would
have worked.** Every static system is a decidable approximation of "this program does not go
wrong", and since the real property is [[Undecidability|undecidable]], the approximation must
be conservative. Some correct programs are refused. The design question for a type system is
not "does it reject good programs" (it must) but "are the ones it rejects programs you wanted
to write".

Types also cannot catch what they cannot express: `head []` is well typed and still crashes,
and a sort function that returns its input unchanged type-checks perfectly. Types constrain
shape, not meaning, which is why [[Program Correctness]] is a separate topic in this course.

## Types as documentation

In a language with [[Parametric Polymorphism]] the signature often pins the implementation
almost completely. `f :: a -> a` can only be the identity function: `f` knows nothing about `a`,
so it cannot construct one, and the only value of type `a` available is the argument. Reading a
Haskell signature tells you far more than reading a Java one, and that is the practical reason
signatures get written even though [[Type Inference]] makes them optional.

## Core Facts to Know

- Static: types are checked before the program runs and errors are compile-time.
- Dynamic: values carry types and errors surface at the moment of execution.
- Static/dynamic, strong/weak, and explicit/inferred are three independent axes.
- [[C]] is statically but **weakly** typed: a cast defeats the check.
- Haskell is statically and strongly typed with no cast, so its guarantees hold at run time.
- Type checking is a conservative approximation, so it necessarily rejects some correct programs.
- It cannot catch what the types do not express: `head []` type-checks and crashes.
- Changing a signature makes the compiler enumerate every affected call site.
- A polymorphic signature constrains the implementation: `a -> a` can only be `id`.
